one_liner: AES-round-based 256-bit-key AEAD for 6G; ~5x OpenSSL AES-256-GCM at 16 KB on one laptop, much less elsewhere.
what_it_does: Rocca (University of Hyogo and KDDI Research, IACR ToSC 2021(2), FSE 2022) is a new nonce-based AEAD, not an AES-GCM implementation, with a 256-bit key, 128-bit nonce and 128-bit tag, aimed at 100+ Gbps single-core software encryption for beyond-5G/6G links. It cannot interoperate with AES-GCM peers. The only first-party code is the C/AES-NI reference in Appendix C of ePrint 2022/116: a streaming rocca_init / rocca_add_ad / rocca_encrypt / rocca_decrypt / rocca_tag API over a rocca_context. The paper also defines a raw encryption-only mode with no AD and no tag.
how_it_is_fast: The 1024-bit (128-byte) state holds eight 128-bit words, and each round spends 4 independent aesenc and 4 128-bit XORs, absorbing 32 bytes of message. Every aesenc sits on its own short critical path, so the round pipelines well on AES-NI or ARMv8 AES units. The designers found this layout by searching a wider space of round functions than Jean and Nikolic's (FSE 2016), including a cost-free word permutation. Each 32-byte ciphertext block adds only 2 more AES rounds for keystream, instead of the ~14 per 16 bytes that AES-256-CTR needs plus GHASH.
when_to_use: Benchmarking or research on AES-round-function AEADs (AEGIS, Tiaoxin, Rocca-S, HiAE), where Rocca is a standard point of comparison.

Bulk AEAD of 8 KB and larger messages on AES-NI x86 or ARMv8 cores in a closed system you control at both ends. At 16 KB it led OpenSSL AES-256-GCM on every CPU in the paper, by 1.5x (i9-11900) to 5.9x (i9-10910), and on every x86 CPU in HiAE's independent tests (e.g. 250.16 vs 51.90 Gbps on a Ryzen 9 7950X).
Pre-VAES Intel servers (Cascade Lake, Haswell class), where HiAE's own Table 10 puts Rocca ahead of HiAE on large messages (Xeon Gold 6242R: 156.60 vs 133.19 Gbps AEAD at 16 KB).
Raw encryption-only use (keystream mode with no tag): 180.55 Gbps at 16 KB on the i7-1068NG7, versus 58.19 Gbps for AES-256-CTR.
when_not_to_use: Short messages (1 KB and under). Initialization and finalization each run 20 rounds, which the paper equates to about 1280 bytes of input per message. Rocca loses to AES-256-GCM at 256 B and 64 B on the paper's own i9-11900 (13.81 vs 15.57 and 3.68 vs 4.51 Gbps), Apple M1 and A15, and at 64 B on all seven x86 CPUs HiAE tested (e.g. 4.00 vs 12.57 Gbps on a Xeon W9-3495X).

Anywhere key commitment matters (multi-recipient, password-based or message-franking designs). Takeuchi, Todo and Iwata (ToSC 2024(2)) give concrete FROB colliding inputs against the designers' latest version and show that no Rocca version is committing-secure.

Settings where a nonce could repeat. The same paper shows universal forgery with practical data complexity under nonce misuse, even with an ideal keyed finalization. The original design also fell to a 2^128 full key recovery (Hosoyamada et al., ToSC 2022(3)).

Production or compliance use: no standard, no FIPS status, no maintained library. The design has been superseded by Rocca-S, whose IETF individual draft (draft-nakano-rocca-s-06) is marked expired and which also has practical committing attacks (ePrint 2024/901).

Interop with ericlagergren/rocca, the only standalone C implementation. It implements the pre-revision initialization, without the key feedforward (open issue #1 since 2024-10-28), so its ciphertexts do not match the revised cipher that produced the cited numbers.

integration.form: source-drop (C listing in Appendix C of ePrint 2022/116). A third-party alternative is ericlagergren/rocca: include/rocca.h plus src/rocca.c, with one-shot rocca_seal/rocca_open, BSD-3-Clause, original Rocca only.
integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and compiler intrinsics (immintrin.h). ericlagergren/rocca also uses memset_s from the optional C11 Annex K.
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented. The paper never states a compiler or flags. ericlagergren/rocca builds its tests with -O2 -maes and passes the Apple-clang-only '-arch x86_64' flag, which suggests it was developed on macOS.
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AES-NI and SSE2 (the paper's Appendix C). The paper also benchmarks ARM NEON + AES builds on Apple M1, A15 and Snapdragon 888 but does not print them. ericlagergren/rocca supports x86-64 (SSE2 + AES) and ARMv8 (NEON + Crypto) and fails with #error elsewhere.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The reference keeps all state in a caller-owned rocca_context, and ericlagergren/rocca keeps it on the stack per call with only const globals, so separate contexts share nothing.

gotchas: Several incompatible 'Rocca' variants exist. The ToSC 2021 original has no key feedforward. The ePrint revision (last updated 2023-03-16) XORs the key into S[0] and S[4] after initialization; this is the version benchmarked at 150.95 Gbps. An intermediate version added a finalization key feedforward that was later removed. Rocca-S is a separate cipher with a 256-bit tag. Check test vectors against the exact version.

ericlagergren/rocca mishandles partial blocks: rocca_seal copies the tail from the start of the plaintext and AD (memcpy(tmp, plaintext, remain)) and writes the partial ciphertext to dst[0]. Any input longer than 32 bytes that is not a multiple of 32 is therefore processed wrongly, and its tests (64-byte plaintexts, AD of 18 or 32 bytes) never exercise that path.

The paper's streaming reference decrypts before the tag is checked and has no verify function. The caller must compute the tag with rocca_tag and compare it in constant time. Each encrypt or AD call zero-pads its own tail, so only the final chunk may be a non-multiple of 32 bytes.

The headline 5.2x rests on a weak baseline. OpenSSL AES-256-GCM measures 29.08 Gbps on the i7-1068NG7 but 117.60 on the paper's i9-11900 and 57.87 on its i9-12900K, and the baseline numbers are identical to two decimals across ePrint revisions whose OpenSSL version label changes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: libaegis is the deployable choice: it is maintained, and in HiAE's independent Table 10 AEGIS-128L beats Rocca at 1 KB and below on all seven x86 CPUs. HiAE is faster than Rocca on VAES-era CPUs, and Rocca is about 5x SNOW-V-GCM. Pick Rocca only for research baselines or large-message bulk encryption on pre-VAES Intel servers, and only if its committing and nonce-misuse weaknesses are acceptable.
verified_claims_summary: The authors built Rocca into OpenSSL 3.1.0-dev and ran it single-threaded on an Intel i7-1068NG7 with 13-byte AD; compiler and flags are not stated. Rocca reached 150.95 Gbps AEAD at 16 KB, versus 29.08 Gbps for OpenSSL AES-256-GCM and 7.60 for ChaCha20-Poly1305. These are numbers for the revised, key-feedforward Rocca; the peer-reviewed ToSC 2021 original reported 138.22 vs 30.59 / 7.57 Gbps, and on the paper's i9-11900 the margin shrinks to 175.12 vs 117.60 Gbps.
status_note: Abandoned as a design, usable only as a reference. The authors' last revision is dated 2023-03-16, the successor Rocca-S's IETF draft is expired, and the only standalone C code (ericlagergren/rocca, BSD-3-Clause, 5 stars) was last committed 2022-01-28, implements the pre-revision cipher, and has an unanswered issue saying so.
